Approximately one year ago, Dr. Liu made changes to one of my teeth using a spring Hawley retainer without discussing the change with me or asking for my consent. If she had simply asked whether I wanted that tooth adjusted, I would have said no because I was satisfied with its position.

Instead, the retainer pushed my tooth backward, and I have now been dealing with pain in that tooth for an entire year. In addition to the physical discomfort, I have spent significant time traveling back and forth to appointments, paying for Uber rides, rearranging my schedule, and waiting for the issue to be corrected.

To make matters more concerning, another orthodontist in the same office told me that my tooth was fine and that he would not have made the adjustment that Dr. Liu made. That only reinforced my belief that this unnecessary change could have been avoided.

After I brought my concerns to the office manager, they agreed to remake my retainer. However, when I arrived for my appointment today—after taking the time to travel to the office—I was informed that the new retainer had been lost. When I called the next morning, I was told the charge was primarily for X-rays. I asked if I could provide recent X-rays from my previous dentist, and I was told that would be acceptable. However, my original appointment was at 9:30 AM—the same time my previous dentist’s office opened—making it impossible to obtain them beforehand. Initially, I was told my appointment could not be moved, and staff claimed I had only provided my insurance information three days earlier, which was not true. I had provided my insurance information multiple times and had been waiting months for this appointment.

After speaking with the office manager, she rescheduled my appointment to 7:00 PM and told me she would contact my previous dentist to obtain my X-rays. I appreciated her willingness to help at the time.

Unfortunately, that effort never materialized. I ultimately obtained the X-rays myself and sent them to the office, but I was then told they were not sufficient and that I would still need new X-rays. The office offered a 20% discount, but I would still have been responsible for approximately $155 out of pocket.

The biggest issue for me wasn’t the cost—it was the lack of communication and follow-through. I spent considerable time trying to resolve this in advance, made multiple phone calls, obtained my own records, and still ended up without a workable solution. After this experience, I decided to cancel my appointment.

I understand that diagnostic requirements and insurance coverage can vary, but patients deserve clear communication, accurate information, and follow-through on commitments. I have been putting off jumping back into working out since I have left the military. As a disabled veteran, it can be difficult to motivate myself to get into the things like exercise, etc. Last week I decided to go all in and I purchased the Vibranium membership (20 classes & 2 Guest Passes/mo) and went to my first class on Mar 10. As of Mar 15 I had only not gone one day (rest is important)!

When you enter Harlem Cycle, you walk right into a cozy waiting area and shop that has water bottles, Beyonce-themed candles, healthy snacks, and more! The staff are incredibly kind and make a great effort to remember who you are. All of the items for sale are incredibly reasonable in price for the quality that you get.

The workouts take you to the club, if the club happens to be up some very steep hills. I have now had 4 different people's classes and each one brings its own vibe, but that vibe is always a bop. As someone who /hates/ going to the gym because of the monotony, I really enjoy that I can get lost in the music and vibe while getting enthusiastic encouragement to push myself.

Another nice thing is that there is no skill level requirement. The staff will help you set up your bike, and will constantly encourage  you to listen to your body on how hard to push yourself.

If you were wondering if you should give it a go, this is an excellent place to get your feet wet. Especially Jorge, Ronnie, and Daniel, who always help me out and encourage me to step it up if it looks like I need more of a challenge. [{"Name":"Owen Murphy","ProfilePicture":"https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/a-/ALV-UjWmG2G1Qp99YPxwQ93GpXog1ueH7jClS9OTu_vktkAWNjGMJh171A=s120-c-rp-mo-ba12-br100","Rating":5,"Description":"I did my first class at Barry’s for free with the Corporate Challenge!

I did not have much expectation going into the class, just pictured it as a regular workout class people goto.

However, my perspective changed after completing my first session. Some important aspects to the class I thought was the instructor, the people, and the music.

The instructor tells instruction on what do to for the next workout about every 30 sec. There’s a lot of people, I went to 8:30am class. And the music is played out loud at a decent volume.

All of this coupled together makes the class exciting, interactive, and motivating as you see other people doing the same thing. Everyone is there with the same goal in mind, and NO headphones!

Tribeca at One York was my first doorway in, delayed by Hurricane Sandy, and walking into that studio felt like the beginning of something. I’m pretty sure my first class was with Rebecca Kennedy, and I left blown away, humbled, and very close to throwing up.

Barry’s earns its reputation the hard way: inside the Red Room, the workout becomes a negotiation with your lungs, legs, and pride. It is still brutal, and it takes commitment, usually several classes close together, before you feel even halfway decent in there. Life and budget have kept me away for 18 months, so if I walked into class tomorrow, I know exactly how humbled I would be. The work is punishing, intentional, and never cruel.

The running has always set Barry’s apart: Woodway treadmills made it smoother, sharper, and more athletic than anything else I was doing. I still remember Rebecca using “treaders,” a funny little word that later disappeared from the instructor lexicon and somehow still makes me nostalgic. My favorite class was Butt and Legs; I’m sure Abs and Ass has a smart rationale, but that old format had magic: visible results, better running, real strength, and a more athletic body.

Noho took what hooked me at Tribeca and showed where the brand was going. The studio was larger, the floor plan was better, and the experience felt like the prototype for how Barry’s could scale while keeping its heat. It felt perfectly appropriate that Barry’s Noho sat across from Indochine, as if downtown glamour, discipline, sweat, and scene had agreed to share the same block. Tribeca gave me the origin story; Noho gave me the blueprint.

Barry Jay once said something close to this: Barry’s was like a nightclub without the drugs, alcohol, and traps that can come with those environments. That has always felt right to me: the dark room, the music, the bodies, and the energy dialed up and down like treadmill speed. Barry’s carried me through marathon training, brutal work seasons, and bosses I will be diplomatic about here. More than once, it helped me keep getting up and keep going when life made that incredibly difficult.

Some mornings, the Red Room did more for my sanity than coffee, a calendar full of high profile meetings, or a well meaning pep talk ever could. I would run, lift, sweat through all of my clothes, and walk back into the city feeling more like myself. Watching the brand grow has been its own pleasure: Barry’s retained instructor quality across markets, turned front desk talent into coaches, earned recognition in smaller cities, and moved its merch upmarket. I worked uptown around the investment circles that eventually backed Barry’s, and I remember seeing the pitch book before North Castle’s investment. Barry Jay’s class at Tribeca, and the original West Hollywood studio with beige linoleum tile and tiny beige lockers, reminded me that the workout built the brand before the brand became glossy.

Instructor shoutout, because the people are the product (alphabetical by first name):

Alycia S, Amanda A, Amber R, Ashley P, Barry J, Bobby M, Brady D, Brendan T, Casey F, Chris H, Erick W, Jake G, Jason R, Jay C, Jennifer S, Joe A, Josey G, Layla L, Lindsey C, Luke S, Matt G, Matt N, Matty M, Max K, Michael P, Mike E, Natalie R, Niv Z, Omri R, Patrick F, Rebecca K, Sarah O, Tiana O, Todd M, and William P.

This is my South of 14th Street thank you note, even knowing other studios and instructors deserve recognition. Barry’s kept me current, connected to younger city life, and loyal to excellent coaching inside a room full of people quietly deciding not to quit. Covid changed the rhythm for a while, but when I returned later, Barry’s felt like Barry’s again, and I will always be thankful for the Red Room and the strange magic of walking in exhausted and leaving restored. I primarily attend the women’s strength classes, and I occasionally take some of the other offerings like co-ed strength + conditioning and restore classes. Even though I had lifted before, I was intimidated to come to my first class. Tight-knit women’s fitness communities can either be incredibly welcoming or feel very cliquey, and Grassroots was such a breath of fresh air from the very beginning.

The community is warm, supportive, and genuinely encouraging - not cliquey at all. Seasoned members are always helping newer members learn the ropes, and everyone really does cheer each other on. It is the kind of place where people notice your progress and celebrate your wins.

The coaches are somehow able to balance teaching new members while still challenging seasoned members, without making anyone feel held back or left behind. There is clearly a science and method to their magic, but they make it look effortless. I can promise you there is so much thought that goes into the workout formula for every class.

What really sets Grassroots apart is how intentional they are about teaching proper form, technique, and the “why” behind each movement. The 6-week “off-the-bar” series is a perfect example — it is designed to build the skills and body awareness needed to perform better during the 8-week “on-the-bar” series. Instead of just pushing you to sweat or lift heavier, the coaches help you understand what each movement is doing, what you should be focusing on, and how to move in a way that supports your body.

I had gone to a different lifting gym years ago and often felt like I was constantly getting injured or chasing a good workout without really understanding my body. Grassroots has been completely different. I feel stronger, more confident, and much more connected to how my body works.

And on top of all of that, it is genuinely fun. The space is beautiful, the equipment is top-notch, the music is great, the teachers bring such good energy, and even the swag is fun. It feels like a place you actually want to show up to, not a place you have to drag yourself to.

They also offer resources like InBody scans, and they take the time to walk you through what every part of the scan means — not just the number on the scale. That level of education and support has helped me feel like I’m finally taking my power back.

Grassroots is more than just a gym. The location is excellent, the studio is always clean and bright, and the ride room itself is big, open, and high-ceilinged.

That extra space really matters. SoHo had incredible downtown energy, but the basement locker rooms were tiny, and NoHo gives you much more breathing room before and after class. It still has that New York SoulCycle charge, just with a little more room to settle in, change, reset, and actually enjoy the full experience.

I took Ariel’s class last August and had a great ride. One of the coolest parts of watching this community over time has been seeing front desk team members and riders grow into instructors, so shoutout to Ariel, Sophia, and Yavuz. I was also a longtime Akin and Yavuz rider, and I remember Yavuz before he started teaching, so seeing that path evolve into the AARMY program has been awesome.

One of the things I appreciate most about studio cycling is how accessible it is for people of all fitness levels. It can be incredibly difficult if you really push, but it also works for group fitness rookies who want structure, music, coaching, and a way to build cardiovascular and muscle strength over time. Studio cycling was my first real group fitness format back in 2007, and nearly 20 years later, SoulCycle still gives me that reset: clip in, ride hard, clear my head, and leave better than I arrived.

7 months into my membership, towards the end of the pandemic, I needed to move across the country for personal reasons.

I intended to continue my membership remotely, but shortly after that they ended online classes.

I called to end my membership - I was willing to pay the cancellation fee and anything else they wanted. But, because I wasn't sure if I was returning or not, they kindly gave this option:
1. end you membership now and pay a fee
or,
2. continue to pay your membership and freeze the time just in case I return. If I don't return, they'd happily refund the time minus the cancellation fee.

I went with the more flexible option so if I came back I did not feel like I wasted money canceling. That was a mistake.

Fast forward to now, and I'm sure I won't return so I called for a refund. Now they suddenly don't do refunds.

So, just paid for 5 months of a membership I can't use, which is exactly what I tried to avoid.

Currently attempting to donate the amount to someone at the gym so it doesn't just go unused.

The gym and instructors are great, management and membership rules are brutal.
______

Before starting at X93 almost 3 years ago I was told that I needed a full knee replacement surgery. My knees were locking, unstable, and limiting what I could do day-to-day. Chris took the time to understand my specific challenges and designed a strength program that safely rebuilt the muscles supporting my knees. Over time, my pain decreased, my stability improved, and I regained confidence in my movement. Thanks to his expertise and careful coaching, I’ve been able to avoid knee replacement surgery — something I honestly didn’t think would be possible.

Beyond my knees, my overall body strength has increased dramatically. I’m stronger, and more balanced. Chris emphasizes proper form, functional strength, and sustainable progress. Every workout is intentional, challenging, and tailored to help you improve safely.

The true proof of how effective this training has been came recently when I had a fall coming down the steps of an airplane overseas. It was one of those moments that could have easily resulted in a serious injury. Instead, I was able to catch myself and walk away with only stitches on my leg. In that moment, I realized just how much strength training has protected me. The stability, muscle strength, and body awareness I’ve developed at X93 made all the difference.

Chris is knowledgeable, encouraging, and genuinely invested in his clients..The gym is immaculately clean and he and Anthony have succeeded in attracting a friendly and diverse clientele who help make the often dreaded and hard workout much less painful.

Not only am I now flying pain-free, but my strength, stability, and body awareness have improved so much that I can comfortably train on the trapeze three days in a row and still feel strong. My flying has noticeably improved, and I feel more capable and confident every time I step onto the rig.

What I love most is that Liberated Fitness focuses on what actually matters. You don't have to pay for fancy locker rooms, expensive weight machines, or overpriced memberships. They have everything you truly need to build a strong, resilient body that feels good to live in.

The coaches genuinely know what they're doing. Every workout is thoughtfully tailored to your individual goals, strengths, and limitations. They take a holistic approach to fitness, helping you move better, prevent injuries, and become stronger in ways that translate to everyday life and whatever sport or activity you love.

On top of that, it's an amazing local community right next to the park. The people are welcoming, supportive, and passionate about helping you succeed.

I was so delighted to be invited to the CycleBar New York, to Rock The Ride, as they say … I guess my hard core cycling reputation got around town !

As a journalist cum cyclist this was a fabulous way to start my day in keeping with my cycling routine of decades …

What struck me about this fabulous Upper East Side rhythm cycling location was the infectious enthusiasm and energy of their reception staff and all training staff.  How warm, welcoming plus professional they were to members and newcomers.

The cycling centre is pretty much configured and designed like most cycling facilities I’ve been too. Nothing fancy but clean and comfortable.

I cycle like a banshee, often doing two to three classes per day, so I know if a cycling operation is a good thing and a worthwhile workout. CycleBar absolutely is …

What I liked about my workout with their instructor Lynsey, over and above her innate ability as a trainer, was her warmth and friendliness as a cycling coach plus the use of a bar/ baton as a weight arm training technique. I’d never experienced this baton training technique before in all my decades of spinning. It was innovative and refreshing. My triceps were lapping it up! I’ll be back for more with Cycle Bar for sure …

A few other things I like about this cycle center are: their in-house cycle shoes being provided on the spot. Saves you lugging your own pair around the city, plus they have small sizes for petite feet like mine. Plus they have gyms all over the city from downtown to uptown (Upper East Side, Noho, Nomad and FlatIron) so pick your cycle spot in the city and rhythm ride with CycleBar.

CycleBars class packages range from USD 49 (for a three pack new riders pass) to USD 279 for a one month unlimited ride.

I wholeheartedly recommend this fitness center to you. They’ll spin you right round into shape in no time with a smile and exceptional professionalism! Second, the front desk staff was unhelpful, and it seems to be a recurring issue across locations. This was my first time experiencing SoulCycle, and although I had read some negative reviews beforehand, I assumed they might be outdated or exaggerated. Unfortunately, after trying it myself, I can understand where those concerns came from.

The instructor for the class, Addie, had an energetic presence during the workout. However, I found her demeanor to feel somewhat impersonal and unwelcoming. As a first-time rider, I expected at least a brief introduction or some guidance, but that didn’t happen. After class, there was also no acknowledgment or follow-up. No one assisted me with setting up my bike, and the class itself felt disorganized at times. The bathrooms were not as clean as expected, the studio felt worn, and several bikes appeared to be in poor condition.

I didn’t expect to be writing a review like this, but my overall experience left me feeling uncomfortable and disappointed. I would encourage others to explore different cycling studios that may offer a more welcoming and supportive environment.

Another unusual aspect was the candle-blowing ritual at the end of class, which felt out of place and unnecessary.

What makes this more frustrating is that the company promotes inclusivity and community, yet my experience did not reflect those values.

At first glance, the space may seem small, but don’t let its size fool you — this is a high-energy, results-driven environment where you can get an amazing workout!

The class had around 12 participants, which I found to be a perfect size. During the session, we rotated through various stations, engaging in circuit training that targeted different techniques. It was a fantastic way to keep things dynamic and challenging. The energy in the room was palpable, and even with a full class, the workout felt personalized.

One of the standout features of my experience was Coach Thor. His passion for martial arts shines through in everything he does. You can sense that he truly breathes, eats, and sleeps this sport. He is incredibly knowledgeable and dedicated, and it shows in the way he interacts with each member of the class. If he notices that you have some skills or potential, he will enthusiastically adjust and introduce new techniques, ensuring that you get the most out of every session. I appreciated his attention to detail and encouragement — it made a significant difference in my workout.

The atmosphere at Hot Fit NYC is also worth mentioning. It’s a welcoming and friendly space where everyone seems to be there for the same reason: to improve their fitness and techniques. This sense of community really motivated me and made the experience much more enjoyable.

While the class was excellent, I did notice that in a bigger group like this one, it can be challenging for the coach to provide individualized feedback to everyone. This is why I would absolutely consider signing up for a private session in the future. I believe that the one-on-one attention would allow me to refine my skills even more effectively and gain a deeper understanding of the techniques we practice.

In terms of conditioning, I can confidently say that if you attend 3-5 classes at Hot Fit NYC consistently, you’re going to see a noticeable improvement in both your fitness level and martial arts skills. The pace and intensity of the class are designed to push you, which is exactly what I was looking for. I walked away from my kickboxing class feeling invigorated and fully energized.

Overall, my experience at Hot Fit NYC was nothing short of fantastic. From the quality of the workout and the expertise of the coach to the supportive environment among participants, I am thoroughly impressed. If you’re looking for an impactful way to get in shape while diving into the world of martial arts, I highly recommend checking out Hot Fit NYC. I also appreciate that Jonathan is able to meet complexity. This work has helped me not only become stronger physically, but also more present, more boundaried, and more honest with myself.

There is compassion in his approach, but also accountability. That combination is rare. I think the women who benefit most from this work are not necessarily looking for someone to count reps and tell them to push harder. * Keep everything in writing. Follow up calls and conversations by email wherever possible.

* Take detailed move-in photos. Photograph every room, including close-ups of marks, stains, scratches, and existing damage.

* Review the Entry Condition Report carefully and dispute anything inaccurate within the required timeframe.

* Attend the exit inspection yourself and take your own photos. Bring a copy of the Entry Condition Report to compare against the property's original condition.

* Know your bond rights. In NSW, tenants can lodge their bond claim online after vacating the property. You do not need to wait for the agent to complete the exit inspection first.

* If an agent or landlord wants to claim part of the bond, they generally need evidence to support it, including documentation, quotes, proof that repairs were completed, and evidence that any damage goes beyond fair wear and tear.

* Understand fair wear and tear and depreciation. Older paint, carpet, and fittings are not treated the same as brand-new items.

* If there is a disagreement, stay calm, organised, and factual. NCAT exists to resolve disputes based on evidence.

* Time and cost matter. Preparing evidence, attending mediation, obtaining quotes, and pursuing NCAT action takes significant time and money for agents and landlords as well. In many cases, the cost of pursuing a relatively small bond dispute can outweigh the amount being claimed. If you are organised, prepared, and willing to participate in the process, your position becomes much stronger.

My biggest advice: document everything carefully from day one. As consistent with other negative reviews for this office, the customer service and patient care is horrendous. I was in contact with the assistant general manager at this office and she was incredibly unprofessional and rude. If she is a reflection of this office's culture and vision, there is absolutely zero care for patients and their needs. I understand you are running a business, but at the end of the day, you are a medical provider that ought to communicate with decency and have some semblance of caring for people .. as people. I felt incredibly dehumanized when I was speaking with this assistant general manager.

The assistant general manager is refusing care because I asked for clarification on why they were charging me a comprehensive ortho fee when I likely have less than a year of treatment left (currently on Invisalign but am looking to move offices and providers because I was not happy with my current provider). I was looking to come back to this office because Dr. Chiang had originally started my case three years ago at the original office I was at. I asked the assistant general manager if she could provide more clarity on why MBO was not able to charge a fairer price for my treatment as I've already been on Invisalign for nearly three years and should be at the tail-end of my treatment. She gave me vague answers (as well as the staff sometime last year) which led us to talking in circles. We ended the convo with me asking if she could see if they could do anything about the cost (I asked respectfully and would have accepted MBO's final answer either way). We ended the call amicably with her apologizing for her tone and demeanor.

Instead, a few days later she calls back and says its in her authority to deny me treatment. Felt pretty blind-sided by her call because this is not where we had left things off. She refused to really provide any explanation as to why she was refusing treatment, but said that she had been thinking about our phone call for a couple days (maybe because I have a valid point in my concerns and ask about the price???). She was really nasty to deal with on this phone call and kept insisting she owed me zero explanation as to why she was refusing treatment. My sense is that it's because I asked if they would consider adjusting the price. Refusing treatment for this reason seems very petty and I wonder if this response is a reflection of MBO's lack of respect for patients. I mean you can even see how the head ortho has responded to other negative reviews. Full of defensiveness.

Maybe I'm overstepping here, but I just don't understand why people go into the medical profession if they lack empathy for people. There are many other ways to make money. Even faster ways to make money without going into medicine. At the end of the day, if you have the audacity to treat patients with disrespect and no care for their medical needs, you really shouldn't be in medicine. I say this because at the end of our phone call, I explained I hadn't seen an ortho since last summer and if she had any other recommendations for a different ortho, she just flat out said no and said "I'm not sure why you're still talking to me". I sent them a new letter with the requested letterhead from my doctor, as well as my travel itinerary, and then they went radio silent, despite repeated follow ups. In that time, I noticed that not only was I charged for the month of May, but there were also three attempted charges for the three months I had been away, trying to be retroactively billed to my card. Absolutely INSANE. I called, and upon speaking to someone in person it was clear that she didn’t know that this had happened and was generally unaware of the new charges, but she did say that they still wouldn’t accept my new letter, without giving a clear reason why.

They’re competent, but nothing extraordinary.

A) S101’s website claims that the sensei, Jonathan Ruiz, created fighters who have fought in the UFC, ONE Championship, Bellator, and similar organizations, but this seems grossly exaggerated.

I only found two Bellator fighters with losing or near-losing records, plus an alleged brief training stint with Uriah Hall, which Hall has never confirmed. Nothing else.

Ruiz likely trained a young-Uriah a few times, rather than having actually “created” him into a UFC-caliber fighter, as his website implies.

B) My experience training there was brief.

The environment came across as unfriendly and unwelcoming, especially as someone coming from another gym. During sparring, I had a round with an instructor who kept escalating the intensity far beyond what was normally expected. I later saw this same exact instructor slam one of the more calm and respectful guys for no reason, in a kickboxing round…. The guy who got slammed doesn’t go hard, from what I remember. He’s a cool dude. There’s a lack of emphasis on proper sparring etiquette here.

I mostly looked to “flow spar” and save the hard rounds for 1 day a week, like many gyms do. But almost everyone I sparred with tried to turn it up. I’d throw a very light leg kick to show them I was calm, and like 98% of them would come back with much harder kicks.  Interestingly enough, on the few occasions where I started to match their energy, the atmosphere would become tense. Not at all what I was looking for!

C) I was absolutely NOT the best person in the room. But I performed much better than I’d expected, which raised questions about the “elite” level of training. BTW, I have ≈2.5 years of training.

I recall sparring one of the gym’s champions. Seemed a bit anti-social, but overall wasn’t too bad a guy. Before the round, one of the other instructors made a point on a Sunday that anyone going too hard would be sent home.

This champion kept swinging like crazy. I had to repeatedly ask him to cool it (I’ve had similar instances like this with other S101 combatants.. not all of ‘em, though). He had ≈6 years of experience, making his escalation/borderline-immaturity quite surprising.

Eventually, I matched his intensity out of frustration. The round became hard, but I held my own and felt I edged it. I didn’t and shouldn’t have expected to be as competitive as I was against someone presented as a top fighter, especially someone swinging hard with twice my training experience.

I am very confident in my abilities, yes, but at the same time, I 100% expected a clearer gap in skill. Don’t get me wrong, this gym is solidly competent. But respectfully, they just aren’t the word-class, elite gym Ruiz presents them to be.

D) I took a grappling class and rolled with a student who I think competed briefly for the gym as a kickboxer. I stuffed his takedown and mounted him. We were both going fairly light at this point. However, when I mounted him, instead of framing normally, he literally jabbed me in my throat with his index and middle fingers.

Afterwards, when I calmly confronted him about that, he admitted to doing it purposely, and then apologized. I somewhat reluctantly accepted it, but it’s incidents like these which highlight the arrogance and lack of etiquette among most of these S101 combatants, not just him. Oh, and hilariously enough, the grappling instructor said Al Iaquinta was scared to fight him back in the day… Got it 😂😅👍🏻

Bottom line: S101’s culture feels arrogant, evidently because Ruiz builds his fighters up solely through regional-tier organizations, inflates their records, and convinces them they’re elite/world-class when they’re not. That false hype clearly shows in their attitudes. Not hating. Calling what I see.

The first thing that immediately stood out to me was the quality of instruction. The coach wasn’t just demonstrating movements — they were breaking everything down with clarity and intention. Every drill was accompanied by a thoughtful explanation of why it mattered, how it connected to real fight scenarios, and how to execute it safely and effectively. Their passion for Muay Thai is obvious, but what impressed me even more was their commitment to making sure every student — beginner or advanced — genuinely understands the technique. This is the kind of teaching that builds real skill, real confidence, and long-term progress.

A Studio That Feels Like Family

The environment at Zombie Muay Thai is incredibly welcoming. From the moment I stepped in, I felt embraced by the community. There’s no ego here — just encouragement, respect, and a shared love for the art. Experienced members go out of their way to support newcomers, and that level of camaraderie is rare in martial arts gyms. Whether you're walking in with zero experience or years of training, you’ll feel like you belong.

A Workout That Pushes You & Leaves You Better

Muay Thai has a reputation for being intense, and this class delivered in all the right ways. The drills were challenging but accessible, and the coach provided thoughtful modifications when needed. I left drenched, energized, and already excited for my next session.

This morning, I took the Warrior Class at Zombie Muay Thai, and I have to say: this class is something special.
This is the closest thing I’ve found in the U.S. to the fighter mobility and conditioning classes I experienced in Asia — and, honestly, it might even be better.

The Warrior Class is a beautifully structured hour that blends:

Mobility training for fighters

Strength conditioning tailored to the demands of Muay Thai

Core stability work that every striker needs

Full range-of-motion drills within proper fight stance

Strengthening of weaker links like wrists, ankles, and stabilizers

Movement patterns that reduce injury and increase explosive power

This isn’t just a workout — it’s a complete system designed to prepare you to fight, move, and recover like an athlete. Everything had intention behind it. Everything felt functional. Everything connected directly to real Muay Thai performance.

By the end of class, I walked out feeling stronger than ever — grounded, stable, mobile, and powerful. It genuinely elevated my entire understanding of how a fighter’s body should move and be trained.

A Class That NEEDS To Be on the Schedule More Often

Right now, the Warrior Class is only offered on Mondays, and I truly hope the gym considers adding it multiple times per week. This is exactly the type of training that helps fighters prevent injuries, move efficiently, improve endurance, and build the foundational body mechanics necessary to level up.

If you’re serious about your Muay Thai journey, this class is essential.

⭐ Final Thoughts ⭐

Zombie Muay Thai delivers on every front — instruction, community, intensity, technique, and now, with the Warrior Class, world-class functional training that rivals elite gyms in Thailand and beyond.

Their passion for Muay Thai is obvious, but what impressed me even more was their commitment to making sure every student — beginner or advanced — genuinely understands the technique. This is the kind of teaching that builds real skill, real confidence, and long-term progress.

The environment at Zombie Muay Thai is incredibly welcoming. From the moment I stepped in, I felt embraced by the community. There’s no ego here — just encouragement, respect, and a shared love for the art. Experienced members go out of their way to support newcomers, and that level of camaraderie is rare in martial arts gyms. Whether you're walking in with zero experience or years of training, you’ll feel like you belong.

Mobility training for fighters

Strength conditioning tailored to the demands of Muay Thai

Core stability work that every striker needs

Full range-of-motion drills within proper fight stance

Strengthening of weaker links like wrists, ankles, and stabilizers

Movement patterns that reduce injury and increase explosive power

This is exactly the type of training that helps fighters prevent injuries, move efficiently, improve endurance, and build the foundational body mechanics necessary to level up.

If you’re serious about your Muay Thai journey, this class is essential.
